newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Dozens of top Russian officials await fate.
newsitem.headline: Dozens of top Russian officials await fate.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin were to hammer out the details of a government reshuffle on Thursday as dozens of top Russian officials wait to be told their fate.

Remarks by the president and the prime minister over the last week have made clear they want a streamlined and efficient new cabinet in which First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais will play the key role in economic reforms.
Kremlin rumours say many ministers and deputy premiers will be axed to make way for a team of Chubais supporters.

Many of the leaks appeared to stem from the Chubais camp in a bid to increase pressure on Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin, sources said. It was not clear to what extent the president and the prime minister would agree on the expected changes.

The idea is to move away from the Soviet style of government, with a minister or a deputy premier in charge of an industry or a sector, and move to an efficient and smaller cabinet with members monitoring key areas of reform.
If this idea prevails, Yeltsin will have to sacrifice or find new roles for several of his long-term allies now in the government and ignore resistance from powerful industrial lobbies.
Three first deputy prime ministers will definitely be demoted to leave Chubais the sole man with the title, and it is unknown whether they will stay in the government at all.

Alexei Bolshakov, a former industrial manager now in overall charge of industry and closely linked to a controversial high speed railway project between Moscow and St Petersburg, is likely to be sacked.
Viktor Ilyushin, in charge of the social sphere, clearly has a poor record and may be sacked also, despite his close personal links to Yeltsin whom he served as a senior aide for many years.

Vladimir Potanin, a youthful former commercial banker, is now in overall charge of the macro-economy. Chubais will take charge of this area, but Potanin, enjoying support from powerful financial groups, could be given another position.
Nine deputy prime ministers are also wondering about their future, most notably Alexander Livshits, who is also finance minister. Despite being a reformer, he is expected to be axed.
Most reports say Livshits will be replaced by Alexei Kudrin, a close Chubais associate who now serves as deputy head of the Kremlin administration which Chubais headed until last Friday.

Most leaks and reports say only four or five deputy prime ministers will be kept. The one most likely to stay in his post is Anatoly Kulikov, who is also interior minister. Kulikov will retain his task of fighting economic crime.

Two close Chubais lieutenants are reported to be set for promotion. Alfred Kokh, who heads the State Property Committee or privatisation agency, which he took over from Chubais, is considered a likely new deputy prime minister.
So is Pyotr Mostovoy, who also worked with Chubais in the Property Committee and who now heads Russia's Bankruptcy Agency.
One of the deputy premiers will be in charge of natural monopolies, a field Yeltsin has pledged to reorganise.
Almost sure to leave is deputy prime minister Vladimir Babichev, in charge of administrative matters.
Among the 20-odd ministers whose fate remains in the balance are Yevgeny Yasin, in charge of the economy, Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and Defence Minister Igor Rodionov.

Yasin, former teacher of Chubais, is likely to stay in his post. So is Primakov, a tough and low-profile minister whom Yeltsin will sorely need at a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton next week in Helsinki.
The future of Rodionov looks less certain after Yeltsin told him earlier this month to stop "whining" about the poor state of the army and get down to work on long-delayed military reform.
